passage: I'm Siddharth, and I shared a flat with Anjali in our final year. I noticed her doing something odd: every morning she stood outside the college gate counting students buying breakfast. She told me the only canteen opened at nine, but first classes started at eight. "People are hungry," she said. She started with twenty packets of poha, made in our kitchen, sold at the gate for a small price. She sold out in fifteen minutes. The next week she made forty. She kept a notebook: cost of rice, oil, onions, packets, and what she earned. Some days she made barely anything. She adjusted the price. I didn't know if she'd keep going, but by the end of term she was earning enough to pay her own phone bill.

qa.q: How many packets of poha did Anjali start with?
qa.a: She started with twenty packets.

qa.q: What might Anjali have felt on days she made barely anything?
qa.a: She may have felt discouraged, but adjusting the price suggests she stayed determined and practical.

qa.q: What did Anjali do that shows basic business sense?
qa.a: She spotted an unmet need, tested it cheaply with a small batch, and tracked costs against earnings to adjust her price.

qa.q: How might the students at the gate see Anjali's poha stall?
qa.a: They'd likely be grateful for a quick, affordable breakfast before early classes.

grounding: A flatmate observes a young woman spotting an unmet need, testing an idea cheaply and tracking revenue and cost.

passage:
Week one: Payal noticed that students in her hostel often had nowhere to print documents late at night. She thought of buying a printer and charging per page. Her friend Chetan warned, "What about ink and paper costs?" Payal waved it off.

Week three: She borrowed an old printer from her uncle and tested the idea for a week, keeping track of every page. She was busy every night. But when she added up the cost of ink and paper, she'd barely broken even. She was frustrated. Chetan helped her see she was charging too little.

Week six: She raised the price slightly and bought paper in bulk. Now she made a small profit each week, and nobody complained.

qa.q: Who lent Payal the printer?
qa.a: Her uncle lent her an old printer.

qa.q: Why was Payal frustrated in week three?
qa.a: She had been busy every night, but after adding up costs she found she'd barely broken even.

qa.q: What business lessons did Payal learn?
qa.a: She learned to test the idea cheaply first and to compare revenue with real costs like ink and paper before setting her price.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel about Payal's success?
qa.a: He might feel pleased his early warning and help with pricing were useful, and happy for her.

grounding: It shows a young woman spotting a need, testing an idea cheaply and learning revenue versus cost over several weeks.

passage: Devika, you want to start a business? Good. Let me tell you about my student Vinita. At twenty, she noticed that the older ladies in our colony struggled to carry vegetables from the market. She thought: what if I deliver? But she didn't borrow money or buy a scooter. She started with her own cycle and five customers. She wrote every expense in a small notebook: tyre repairs, bags, her own time. After a month, she saw she was earning less than she spent. So she started charging a small delivery fee and grouping orders by lane. The ladies didn't mind. By the end of the year, she had thirty customers and a second-hand scooter bought with her own savings. Start small, beta. Count everything.

qa.q: How many customers did Vinita start with?
qa.a: She started with five customers.

qa.q: How might Vinita have felt when she saw she was earning less than she spent?
qa.a: She may have felt disappointed or worried, but she chose to adjust instead of giving up.

qa.q: What does the elder advise Devika, and why is it good advice?
qa.a: Start small and count everything, because testing cheaply and tracking costs shows whether an idea can actually make money.

qa.q: How might the older ladies in the colony see Vinita's service?
qa.a: They'd likely be grateful for help with heavy bags and happy to pay a small fee.

grounding: An elder tells a young woman how a student spotted an unmet need, tested it cheaply and understood revenue versus cost.

passage: Siddharth had two thousand rupees and a hunch. Every evening outside the coaching centres in Kota, students queued for bad sandwiches because the hostel canteens closed at seven. 'Home-style dinner boxes,' he told his friend Pradeep. 'People would pay.' Pradeep asked, 'Would they? How many?' Instead of renting a stall, they tested cheaply: Pradeep's aunt cooked twenty boxes of rajma rice, and they sold them from a cycle for three evenings. The first evening, twelve sold. The second, eighteen. On the third it rained, and they sold six. Siddharth sat on the steps doing sums in a notebook: vegetables, gas, boxes, what they paid the aunt. On most boxes they earned barely anything. 'So we need more per box, or cheaper boxes,' he said, frowning but interested. The idea wasn't dead. It just had to add up.

qa.q: What dish did Pradeep's aunt cook for the test?
qa.a: Twenty boxes of rajma rice.

qa.q: What does Siddharth's 'frowning but interested' reaction suggest he felt?
qa.a: He was disappointed the earnings were thin but curious rather than defeated, treating the result as a puzzle to solve.

qa.q: Why was selling from a cycle a smart first step?
qa.a: It checked real demand and real costs cheaply over a few evenings, before spending on a stall, and showed the thin margin early.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's question 'Would they? How many?' have helped?
qa.a: It pushed Siddharth from a hunch towards evidence; a friend asking hard questions is useful before any money is spent.

grounding: Shows a young man spotting an unmet need, testing it cheaply in bad weather and comparing revenue with costs.

passage: In Payal's colony in Secunderabad, the old tailor near the gate had shut his shop in March, and the residents' chat group was full of the same question: 'Anyone know someone for blouse alterations?' Payal's friend Vandana sewed beautifully and wanted to earn a little. 'Before you buy a new machine,' Payal said, 'let's see if people will actually pay.' They posted a simple offer in the group for one weekend only, using Vandana's mother's machine. Fourteen orders came in. Payal kept a sheet: thread, buttons, auto fare for pickups, and the hours Vandana spent. After costs they earned less than Payal expected, mostly because of the auto trips. 'So we ask people to drop things here,' Vandana said. Payal nodded, already redoing the sheet. Real demand, a little real money, and a clear next fix.

qa.q: How many orders came in during the trial weekend?
qa.a: Fourteen orders.

qa.q: Why did Payal want to test the idea before buying a new machine?
qa.a: She was unsure people would actually pay and felt cautious about spending money on a hunch.

qa.q: What did tracking costs reveal, and how did they respond?
qa.a: Auto fares for pickups ate most of the earnings, so they decided to ask customers to drop things off, fixing the cost instead of giving up.

qa.q: How might the colony residents see the new service?
qa.a: As a relief after the tailor closed, since it filled a need they had kept asking about in the group.

grounding: Shows two friends spotting a local need, testing it for one weekend and learning from revenue and costs.

passage:
"Amma, how much for one dabba of your lemon rice and curd?"
Sudha looked up from the stove. "For whom?"
"The PG boys next door. Four of them asked me yesterday where to get home food. Their mess closes at eight."
"And you want to sell my lemon rice."
"Just test it. Ten dabbas, one week. If nobody pays, we eat it."
"What will you charge?"
"Sixty?"
Sudha put down the ladle. "Count first. Rice, curd, oil, gas, the boxes, your time walking over. What does one cost us?"
Chetan scribbled in the newspaper margin. "Around forty-five… if the boxes come back."
"And if they don't?"
He frowned. "Then I lose money on every box."
"So?"
"So steel boxes with a deposit, and I charge seventy."
Sudha smiled. "Now you're a businessman. Ten dabbas. Tomorrow."

qa.q: When does the PG boys' mess close?
qa.a: At eight.

qa.q: What does Chetan's frown suggest when he realises the boxes might not come back?
qa.a: Chetan felt worried and a bit deflated, seeing that his first price could lose money on every box.

qa.q: What makes this a cheap way to test the idea?
qa.a: Only ten dabbas for one week, with the family eating any unsold food, so little is risked while they learn whether people will pay.

qa.q: How does Sudha see Chetan's idea?
qa.a: Sudha takes it seriously but tests it with hard questions about cost, and seems pleased when he thinks it through.

grounding: A young man spots a food need next door and, guided by his mother, tests it cheaply and works out costs before pricing.

passage: In second year I, Naveen, was sure I'd found a gap. Before every exam, everyone in our hostel queued at the one photocopy shop outside the gate. So Asif and I borrowed his uncle's old printer and offered printing inside the hostel at two rupees a page. We bought nothing new; we tested it for one exam week. We got busy fast, forty orders the first night. Then I sat down with a notebook. Ink, paper, the printer jamming twice, our time until 2 a.m. We were making almost nothing on each page. The real surprise was in the orders: half the people wanted the same seniors' notes. So next exam season we stopped printing single pages and sold bound sets of the most popular notes, with the seniors' permission and a share for them. That, finally, covered our costs.

qa.q: How many orders did they get the first night?
qa.a: Forty orders.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when adding up the costs in the notebook?
qa.a: Naveen probably felt disappointed and deflated, finding they made almost nothing despite being busy.

qa.q: What did the one-week test reveal, and how did they use it?
qa.a: Costs nearly ate the income, but half the demand was for the same notes, so they switched to bound sets that covered costs.

qa.q: How might the seniors whose notes were sold see the arrangement?
qa.a: The seniors were asked for permission and got a share, so they'd likely feel respected and pleased their notes helped juniors.

grounding: A student looks back on testing a hostel printing idea cheaply, finding costs too high, and pivoting to what customers really wanted.

passage: Incubation cell, mentor's note, 2 February. Aadhya and Shreya (second-year BBA) pitched a laundry pickup service for the women's hostel. They had noticed that the only washing machines are on the ground floor and the queue runs past ten at night. I asked who had told them they would pay. Nobody yet. They agreed to test before spending: a simple form, a week of pickups carried by hand, a local dhobi doing the washing. Result today: twenty-three sign-ups, eleven repeat orders. Aadhya had worked out that after the dhobi's charge and the auto fare, each bag earned them twelve rupees. Shreya pointed out that their own time wasn't counted. They are now deciding whether to raise the price or batch pickups to two days a week. I'm pleased they are asking the cost question before the logo question. — Dr Menon

qa.q: How many repeat orders did they get?
qa.a: Eleven repeat orders.

qa.q: What might Aadhya have felt on working out twelve rupees per bag?
qa.a: Aadhya probably felt a mix of pride at earning something and worry that the margin was so thin.

qa.q: Why was a one-week test better than spending first?
qa.a: It proved real demand through sign-ups and repeat orders, and showed the true margin, before any money went on equipment or branding.

qa.q: How does Dr Menon see the team's progress?
qa.a: Dr Menon is pleased that they are asking about cost before branding, and sees it as sound business sense.

grounding: A mentor's note shows two students spotting a hostel need, testing it cheaply, and weighing revenue against cost.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Idea! All the PG students near our college eat terrible canteen food or order expensive delivery. What if I sell home-style tiffins?
Jeevan said, "Test it first. Don't rent a kitchen yet."
So this week I made ten tiffins in Ammi's kitchen and sold them in the hostel for Rs 80 each. Sold out in an hour.
Then I counted costs: vegetables, rice, oil, boxes, gas. Rs 60 per tiffin. So only Rs 20 each for me, not counting my time.
I'm excited and a bit deflated. Next week: try a smaller menu, buy vegetables wholesale, and ask people what they'd pay.
— Parveen

qa.a: Jeevan would likely be pleased Parveen tested first and learned about costs early.

passage:
In the village, Arohi noticed that women walked five kilometres to the market for pickles and papad, while Nirmala aunty made the best mango pickle in the district.
"Why don't you sell yours?" Arohi asked.
"Who would buy? And the jars cost money."
Arohi thought. "Let's try twenty small jars first, just in the village."
They sold all twenty in two days. Arohi wrote down every cost: mangoes, oil, spices, jars, labels. The profit was small but real.
"If we reuse jars, costs go down," said Nirmala aunty.
Arohi added a new column: "Returned jars." The next batch made more money.

qa.q: How many small jars did they try first?
qa.a: Twenty small jars.

qa.q: What was Nirmala aunty feeling when she asked "Who would buy?"
qa.a: Nirmala aunty felt doubtful and cautious about the costs.

qa.q: What business steps did Arohi use?
qa.a: She spotted a local need, tested small, wrote down all costs, and found ways to lower costs like reusing jars.

qa.q: How might the village women see the pickle sales?
qa.a: They probably feel relieved not to walk so far and happy to buy good local pickle.

grounding: A village teen spots an unmet need, tests a pickle business cheaply and tracks costs.

passage:
In Berlin, Fatima noticed the same thing every morning at the university: students walking bikes with flat tyres, because the nearest repair shop was far and expensive.
She told her flatmate Jana, "What if we fix tyres on campus?"
Jana was practical. "Before you buy anything, test it."
They borrowed a pump and tools, bought a small box of tubes and patches, and made a sign: "Flat tyre? 10 minutes, Tuesday 8–10." The first Tuesday, three people came. The second, eleven.
Jana made a simple sheet: money in, money out. The tubes and patches cost more than they'd thought. They raised the price slightly for tube replacements and kept patches cheap.
By the end of the month, they'd covered their costs with a little left over. More importantly, they knew people actually wanted it.

qa.q: When did Fatima and Jana run the repair stand?
qa.a: On Tuesdays, from 8 to 10.

qa.q: How do you think Fatima felt when eleven people came the second week?
qa.a: Fatima likely felt excited and encouraged, seeing that the need was real.

qa.q: What basic business lessons does their test show?
qa.a: Spot a real need, test it cheaply before investing, and track costs against income so prices cover what you spend.

qa.q: How might the students with flat tyres see the stand?
qa.a: They would probably feel relieved and grateful to get a quick fix on campus instead of walking far.

grounding: Shows young adults spotting an unmet need, testing it cheaply and learning revenue versus cost.

passage:
At the engineering college in Nagpur, the canteen opened at 9, but first lectures started at 8. Deepika noticed half her hostel skipped breakfast or ate biscuits in class.
She and her friend Jaya asked the warden if they could sell poha and tea from the hostel common room, 7 to 8, as a trial for two weeks. He agreed, as long as it was clean and they cleared up.
They asked twenty students what they'd pay. They bought ingredients for thirty plates the first day. They sold eighteen, and had to throw food away.
Jaya kept a notebook: ingredients, gas, paper plates, and what came in. They cut the next day's batch to twenty and sold all of it.
By the end of the trial they knew their real cost per plate and that Mondays were busiest. The warden asked if they'd continue next term.

qa.q: How many plates did they sell on the first day?
qa.a: They sold eighteen of thirty plates.

qa.q: How might Deepika and Jaya have felt throwing food away on the first day?
qa.a: They probably felt disappointed and a bit worried, seeing the cost of guessing too high.

qa.q: What did Jaya's notebook teach them about the business?
qa.a: It showed their real cost per plate and busiest days, so they could match batch size to demand and avoid waste.

qa.q: How might the warden see their trial by the end?
qa.a: The warden seems impressed and pleased, asking if they would continue next term.

grounding: Illustrates young adults spotting an unmet need on campus, testing it cheaply and understanding cost versus income.

passage:
Dear Ramesh Mama,
You asked about my "tailoring idea". Here's where it's got to.
Remember how Mummy's shop is always full of people who want small alterations but can't come during work hours? I thought: what if I collect clothes from offices at lunch and bring them back the next day?
I didn't want to spend anything big first. I made a simple poster and put it up in two office buildings near the shop. Fourteen people used it in the first two weeks. I walked and took the bus.
I tracked everything: what customers paid, Mummy's share for stitching, my bus fares, the posters. After two weeks I realised the bus fares ate most of what was left, so now I only collect on Tuesdays and Fridays, in one trip.
Can we talk about whether it's worth asking a bank officer about a small loan for a scooter later?
Vinita

qa.q: How many people used the service in the first two weeks?
qa.a: Fourteen people.

qa.q: How does Vinita seem to feel about the idea so far?
qa.a: Vinita seems excited but careful, pleased it's working while watching costs closely.

qa.q: What does Vinita's change to Tuesdays and Fridays show about business sense?
qa.a: It shows Vinita noticed a cost, bus fares, eating the profit and changed the model to cut it.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Mama respond to the loan question?
qa.a: Ramesh Mama might be impressed by the tracking and suggest talking to the bank officer before deciding, rather than rushing.

grounding: Shows a young adult spotting an unmet need, testing cheaply and weighing revenue against costs.

passage: Payal, people think I just woke up with the idea. No. In second year, I, Irfan, kept seeing the same thing at our hostel gate: students waiting forty minutes for the one photocopy shop, which shut at eight. Before spending anything, I put a sign-up sheet on the notice board: "Would you pay for late-night printing in the hostel?" Sixty names in two days. Then I borrowed an old printer from my cousin and ran it from my room for two weeks, three hours a night. I charged two rupees a page. After paper, ink and electricity, I kept about fifty paise a page, much less than I'd imagined. Some nights I earned almost nothing. But I learned where the money actually went. Now the warden has given us a small counter, and we're testing a pre-booking form.

qa.q: How many names were on the sign-up sheet after two days?
qa.a: There were sixty names in two days.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel on nights when the printer earned almost nothing?
qa.a: Irfan was probably disappointed, since the margin was far smaller than imagined, yet curious enough to learn where the money went.

qa.q: Why was the sign-up sheet a smart first step?
qa.a: It tested whether students really wanted late-night printing before any money was spent.

qa.q: How might the students waiting at the hostel gate see the new counter?
qa.a: They would likely feel relieved and grateful to skip a forty-minute queue at a shop that shuts at eight.

grounding: Shows a student spotting an unmet need, testing it cheaply and learning the gap between revenue and cost.
